strengths: Formulating offline model-based RL as a BAMDP is a principled and elegant approach to handling epistemic uncertainty in the learned dynamics ensemble.
The introduction of Continuous BAMCP with Double Progressive Widening (DPW) enables tree search in continuous state and action spaces under model uncertainty.
The proposed search-based policy iteration framework successfully distills MCTS search results into policy and value networks, showing a solid 'RL + Search' implementation.

Excellent empirical results: the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art offline MBRL and model-free baselines on 12 D4RL MuJoCo tasks and 3 highly stochastic tokamak control target tracking tasks.
Extensive ablation studies are provided, isolating the contributions of BAMDP training (BA-MBRL), search (BA-MCTS), and supervised learning distillation (BA-MCTS-SL).
weaknesses: Clarification on Bayes-Adaptivity at Test-Time: There is a contradiction between Footnote 5 (which states that $\pi$ and $V$ are implemented as functions of history $(s, h)$) and the text on page 9 (which states that the policy is a standard feedforward neural network on the state $s$ for real-time execution). If the distilled policy at test-time only takes the physical state $s$ as input, it is memoryless and cannot update or utilize the belief $b(\theta)$ online. This means the final executed policy is not Bayes-adaptive. The authors should clarify this design choice and discuss its implications.

Computational Complexity and Training Time: While the authors report the training times of Sampled EfficientZero (Table 6), they do not explicitly report the training times of their own proposed methods (BA-MCTS, BA-MCTS-SL). Since MCTS in continuous spaces with ensemble dynamics is computationally expensive, providing these training times is crucial for evaluating the practical utility of the method.

Limited Explanation of BA-MBRL's Success: Simply updating the belief $b(\theta)$ during training-time simulator rollouts (BA-MBRL) improves the performance score from 65.16 (Optimized) to 71.06, even when the policy itself is memoryless. The underlying mechanism of why this training-time belief adaptation benefits memoryless policies warrants a deeper intuitive or theoretical explanation.

strengths: Principled Formulation: Modeling offline MBRL under the BAMDP framework is highly principled. It allows the agent to maintain a belief over the learned ensemble models and adapt online within an episode, which is an elegant way to handle epistemic uncertainty in offline settings.

Algorithm Design: The extension of BAMCP to continuous spaces via Double Progressive Widening (DPW) and casting the BAMDP as an MDP solved by PUCT (Continuous BAMCP) is mathematically sound and well-constructed.

Robust Evaluation: The paper evaluates on standard D4RL benchmarks and a highly realistic, stochastic tokamak control simulator. Outperforming state-of-the-art model-based and model-free methods in both domains validates the efficacy of the proposed method.
Clarity and Detail: The paper is very well-written, with detailed pseudocodes (Algorithms 1 & 2), and a thorough appendix addressing design choices, hyperparameter settings, and ablation studies.
weaknesses: Computational Overhead: Although the search is only performed on 10% of the training states, MCTS in continuous spaces is still computationally expensive. The paper would benefit from a direct wall-clock time comparison between BA-MCTS and standard offline MBRL baselines (such as Optimized/MBPO) to clarify the computation-performance trade-off.

Representational Capacity of Ensembles: The belief update relies on a finite ensemble of size K. If all ensemble members make poor predictions on out-of-distribution states (as they are trained on the same static dataset), the posterior belief might become unreliable. A discussion on how this limitation impacts the algorithm's robustness would be helpful.

Incremental Novelty: The primary algorithmic building blocks (BAMDP, DPW/PUCT, ensemble-based reward penalty, and MuZero-like distillation) are established techniques. The main contribution is their specific synthesis for offline MBRL.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important problem in offline reinforcement learning (handling epistemic model uncertainty) by framing it under the principled Bayes Adaptive MDP (BAMDP) framework.

The proposed Continuous BAMCP algorithm is a logical and well-structured extension of BAMCP, successfully incorporating Double Progressive Widening (DPW) and PUCT to accommodate continuous state and action spaces.
The manuscript is written clearly, and the implementation details are well-documented, with comprehensive pseudocode provided for the main planning and policy iteration routines.
The evaluation spans both the standard D4RL MuJoCo suite and a complex, high-dimensional real-world physical simulator (tokamak control for nuclear fusion).
weaknesses: Fundamental Inconsistency in the Bayes-Adaptive Formulation: The core motivation of using a BAMDP is to allow the policy to adapt online to different dynamics based on the interaction history (by updating the belief $b_t$). However, the authors state in Section 5 that at test time, they discard the history/belief and use a simple feedforward neural network $\pi(a|s)$. If the deployed policy cannot access the history $h$ or the belief $b_t$, it is physically impossible for it to perform Bayes-adaptive control. Discarding the history at test time nullifies the primary theoretical benefit of the BAMDP formulation. Furthermore, training a Markov policy $\pi(a|s)$ on BAMDP rollouts (which are non-Markovian due to history-dependent belief updates) is mathematically inconsistent and subjects the policy to partial observability.

Belief Collapse in Continuous Spaces: In Equation (4), the belief update relies on the transition likelihood $P^i_\theta(s'|s, a)$. In continuous state spaces, this likelihood is a probability density. Multiplying densities over successive steps typically leads to extreme numerical instability and 'belief collapse', where the belief concentrates entirely on a single arbitrary model within a few steps. The paper does not analyze or discuss this phenomenon, leaving it unclear whether the belief is truly adaptive or if it quickly degenerates into a one-hot vector.

Unfair Empirical Comparison and Outdated Baselines: The baseline results in Table 1 (Optimized, COMBO, MOReL, MOPO) are copied directly from their original papers rather than being re-run under the same computational budget (training epochs, seeds, and codebase) as the proposed methods. Table 3 shows that the proposed methods are trained for up to 1000 epochs, which is significantly longer than typical offline MBRL training budgets. Additionally, the paper compares only against older baselines (2020–2022) and omits comparison with more recent, stronger model-based offline RL algorithms (such as RAMBO or diffusion-based models).

Computational Complexity: Performing MCTS during training (even at only 10% of states) introduces immense computational overhead. The paper lacks a direct training-time comparison between BA-MCTS and standard offline MBRL (e.g., Optimized) to justify whether the marginal performance improvements outweigh the substantial computational cost.

strengths: Principled Formulation: Framing offline model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) as a Bayes Adaptive Markov Decision Process (BAMDP) is mathematically sound and provides a highly principled mechanism to handle epistemic model uncertainty.

Methodological Contribution: Successfully extends Bayes-Adaptive Monte Carlo Planning (BAMCP) to continuous state and action spaces with stochastic transitions by integrating Double Progressive Widening (DPW) and PUCT. This addresses a major limitation of classical BAMCP.

Thorough Evaluation: Evaluated on both standard D4RL MuJoCo locomotion benchmarks and a highly realistic, stochastic tokamak control simulator for nuclear fusion. The proposed methods (BA-MCTS, BA-MCTS-SL) consistently achieve state-of-the-art performance.

Detailed Empirical Analysis: Provides extensive ablation studies, including analysis of the benefits of belief adaptation over uniform ensembles, comparison with MuZero-type methods, and evaluation of the impact of the pessimistic reward penalties.

No Deployment Overhead: Distilling the search results into policy and value networks via policy iteration ensures that no expensive Monte Carlo Tree Search is needed at test time, making it practical for real-time deployment.
weaknesses: High Training Complexity: Although test-time search is avoided, the training time is exceptionally high. As shown in Table 11, training the MCTS variants can take up to 77 hours, which is an order of magnitude higher than standard model-based offline RL (BA-MBRL).

Hyperparameter Sensitivity: The continuous BAMCP planning and search-based policy iteration introduce many sensitive hyperparameters (such as expansion coefficients, progressive widening parameters, and proportion of state search). As shown in Table 4, these parameters vary significantly across tasks, and tuning them in a purely offline setting can be challenging.

Heuristic Pessimistic Penalty: The reward penalty design (Equation 5) relies heavily on prior ensemble discrepancy techniques (e.g., Lu et al., 2022). While adapted to include belief weights, the underlying mechanism is not fundamentally new.

Lack of Theoretical Analysis: Although the paper references PUCT consistency, it lacks a formal theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees for the joint 'Continuous BAMCP + Policy Iteration' loop under function approximation.

strengths: Principled and well-grounded formulation: Modeling offline model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) as a Bayes Adaptive Markov Decision Process (BAMDP) is a theoretically elegant and principled way to handle the epistemic uncertainty that naturally arises from static datasets.

Insightful theoretical observation on root sampling: The paper identifies a key technical limitation in combining standard Bayes Adaptive Monte Carlo Planning (BAMCP) with Double Progressive Widening (DPW), specifically showing that the classic root sampling trick fails because DPW biases the transition counts inside the search tree. Resolving this by explicitly tracking and updating the belief state during the search is a solid contribution.

Convincing and extensive empirical evaluation: The proposed framework is evaluated on twelve standard D4RL MuJoCo tasks and three highly stochastic tokamak control tasks (nuclear fusion simulation). It consistently outperforms strong, modern baselines such as MOBILE, CBOP, and MuZero-type methods (Sampled EfficientZero).

Thorough analysis and ablations: The paper provides extensive supplementary results, including transition likelihood comparisons (with vs. without belief adaptation), reward penalty ablations, and a detailed breakdown of training times.
weaknesses: High computational cost: As reported in Table 11, training times for the search-based variants can be extremely high (e.g., exceeding 70 hours for some Walker2d tasks on a server with 4 Tesla V100 GPUs). This high training cost may limit the practical reproducibility and adoption of the algorithm by researchers with constrained compute resources.

Hyperparameter complexity: The search process introduces several sensitive hyperparameters (such as progressive widening coefficients $\alpha, \beta$, exploration constant $c$, noise mixture $\eta$, and branch limits $n_a, n_s$). This complexity makes hyperparameter tuning highly non-trivial across different environments.

No test-time search: For real-time execution, the agent relies solely on the distilled policy without performing test-time tree search. While this is practical and necessary for environments like tokamak control, it would be academically interesting to quantify the performance gap between the distilled policy and the actual MCTS planning policy at deployment time.

strengths: The paper introduces a principled framework that models offline model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) as a Bayes Adaptive MDP (BAMDP), offering an elegant and theoretically sound way to handle epistemic uncertainty over learned dynamics models.

It successfully extends Bayes Adaptive Monte Carlo Planning (BAMCP) to continuous, stochastic state-action spaces by integrating Double Progressive Widening (DPW), and incorporates this search operator into an offline policy iteration framework.

Comprehensive and strong empirical results on 12 D4RL MuJoCo tasks and a complex, real-world tokamak control simulator, showing clear superiority over state-of-the-art offline RL and deep-search-based baselines like Sampled EfficientZero.
Excellent ablation studies and qualitative analysis, demonstrating the isolated benefits of both the BAMDP belief adaptation and the deep MCTS planning components.
weaknesses: High computational complexity during training: as shown in Table 11, the training time for BA-MCTS is up to an order of magnitude higher than standard model-based offline RL (BA-MBRL), which might limit its scalability.

The Bayesian posterior belief update assumes the true transition dynamics are within the span of the deep ensemble (a Bayes-closed setup). The paper would benefit from a discussion on how the algorithm behaves when the ensemble is misspecified (e.g., all models are wrong out-of-distribution).

While the improvements are notable, the experiments are evaluated over only 3 random seeds, whereas current standards in RL benchmarking often recommend 5 or more seeds to ensure statistical significance.
